A LITTLE CURIOSITY. A LITTLE SALT WATER.

Because “what if we leave later?”
deserved a better answer.

Built for fun by a controls engineer who likes understanding how things work—and sometimes that turns into a website.

Built for the fun of figuring it out.

This started with a simple question: how much does departure time change a passage? A tide table can tell you what happens at a station. The interesting part is what happens when the boat actually gets there.

The planner brings the pieces together: NOAA predictions, a course, boat speed, and a moving arrival time. Then came the New Jersey inside passage, based on an actual recorded trip—with its slow sections and bridge waits, because boats rarely spend an entire day at their advertised cruising speed.

This project combines engineering, boating and the fun of figuring things out. There is no grand business plan behind it—just something useful for curious boaters to explore.

One part boat trip.
One part engineering experiment.
Several parts “just one more feature.”

A way to explore the timing.

The current planner asks how changing current affects time underway. The inside tide planner asks how much tide is predicted when the boat reaches the priority shallow-water locations. They make it easier to try a different departure, change speed, or add a longer bridge wait and see what moves.

The predictions come from NOAA; the presentation, route timing and estimates are this project’s work. The detailed Help page explains the assumptions, nearby-station tide proxies, bridge checks, map controls and how to read the results.

This is a personal planning experiment. It does not verify a navigable route, water depth, bridge clearance or actual conditions. Use proper navigation tools for those jobs.

Follow the passage, from the map to the briefing.

The tide planner opens on Stay inside, with ocean alternatives available for each visit. Start by setting your boat’s cruising speed. Both planners place Boat information before Passage options and explain that the starting speeds are examples. On the tide planner, this section starts expanded and can be collapsed with its arrow after you check your boat settings.

Named locations in the lists and endpoint dropdowns pan the map to the selected place without changing zoom or rotation. The selected tide-station row stays highlighted while you inspect the map. The last selected map location stays highlighted, with a pulsing ring on the inset map until you choose another location. When the main map has scrolled away, a larger live preview keeps the selected point easy to see. It stays open while you hover over it and closes about four seconds after you move away. Another selection updates it, left-button dragging pans it and the mouse wheel zooms it. The return button takes you to the full map with your pan position and zoom retained. Route overlays, current/tide colors and ordinary marker interactions remain available.

The selected departure display shows the date and time actually used in the calculation, with Eastern daylight or standard time applied. Both trip briefings bring together the passage plan and forecast conditions along it: temperature, wind, gust and precipitation ranges at route positions and estimated encounter times.

For travel between northern inside stops and Atlantic City, the Barnegat–Absecon ocean alternative connects both recorded inlet approaches while keeping the inside portions of the trip. A constructed offshore connector is a planning estimate, not a depth-validated track.

The largest available forecast seas are identified with a nearby named location, coordinates and estimated time. This is the highest sampled significant wave height, not the largest individual wave or a guaranteed maximum. Inside-water waves are not modeled by the tide planner’s offshore forecast. Coverage and missing forecasts are stated explicitly, and forecasts do not change the underlying passage calculations. The weather guide explains the sources and limits.
